senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀγαθοποιέω ‘to do good,’ 88.3) one who customarily does good

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: an association of persons having a strong sense of unity
senses.comment: It is often quite impossible to speak of fellow Christians as ‘the brothers and sisters,’ since a number of receptor languages do not permit this type of extension of meaning from an underlying base meaning ‘brother’ or ‘sister.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to speak of ‘fellow believers’ or ‘those who believe together with others’ or ‘those who likewise believe.’ See also discussion at 11.23.

senses.def: to have the capacity to perceive clearly and hence to understand the real nature of something
glosses: to have the capacity to understand

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀλαζονεία ‘pretentious pride,’ 88.219) one who is pretentiously proud and given to bragging about it
senses.comment: In a number of languages an arrogant person is described figuratively as ‘one who speaks big words about himself’ or ‘one whose mouth is too big for his body.’

senses.def: pertaining to not being concerned or anxious
a lack of sensitivity to what is proper
to bring or lead up
to be carried or borne upward
to offer up someone or something as a sacrifice (a technical term in the sacrificial system)
to engage in an intense struggle against something or someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot use a term in Hebrews 12:4 which would suggest physical struggle, for essentially this is psychological opposition. In some cases the appropriate equivalent would be ‘to do all you can to oppose sin’ or ‘to do everything possible against evil.’

senses.def: to come near to and to meet, either in a friendly or hostile sense
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to specify clearly by the choice of terms whether the meeting is friendly or hostile.

senses.def: to keep safe that which is of great value
senses.comment: There are certain problems involved in the combination of ἀποθησαυρίζοντας and θεμέλιον, for this would constitute a type of mixed metaphor. In some languages, therefore, it may be useful to speak of θεμέλιον in 1 Timothy 6:19 as ‘a help’ or even as ‘something valuable.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to act harshly toward someone
to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
(derivative of ἁρπαγή[a] ‘act of plunder,’ 57.235) that which is taken by force or plundered
a state of strong desire to gain things and, if necessary, by violent means
a position extremely close to another position

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: pertaining to not being able to be seen or known, and thus to be hidden
senses.comment: It is possible to render ‘that can be hidden from him’ as ‘that people can keep God from seeing’ or ‘that people can prevent God from knowing about.’

senses.def: the father of a man killed in the Temple
a strong, destructive force
senses.comment: In some languages it is difficult, if not impossible, to find a term such as ‘violence,’ but one may describe the effects of violence by expressions which indicate the harm that is done. For example, Acts 5:26 may be translated ‘they did not wish to harm anyone, for they were afraid of the people,’ and similarly in Acts 27:41, one may translate ‘the waves did great damage to the stern.’

senses.def: (derivative of βρῶσις[a] ‘eating,’ 23.3) pertaining to what can be eaten
(derivative of γεωργέω ‘to cultivate land,’ 43.1) one who engages in agriculture or gardening
(derivative of δανείζω ‘to lend money,’ 57.209) that which has been loaned

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a group of citizens assembled for socio-political activities
senses.comment: It is possible that in ἐκκλησία[c] there is somewhat more focus upon the people being together as a legal assembly, while in the case of δῆμος the emphasis is merely upon a meeting of citizens. But in the NT one cannot distinguish clearly between the meanings of these two words.|ἐκκλησία[c] and δῆμος may be rendered in some languages as ‘a meeting of the people who belonged to that place’ or ‘… who were inhabitants of that town’ or ‘… whose homes were in that town.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of διαπρίομαι ‘to be sawn through,’ not occurring in the NT) to be angry to the point of rage
(derivative of δικαιόω ‘to act justly,’ not occurring in the NT) a regulation concerning right or just action

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: an act which is in accordance with what God requires
the act of clearing someone of transgression
senses.comment: In a number of languages the process of acquittal takes the form of a direct statement, for example, ‘to say, You are not guilty’ or ‘…, You no longer have sin’ or, as expressed idiomatically in some instances, ‘…, Sin is no longer on your head’ or ‘…, Your sins are now given back to you.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of δράσσομαι ‘to catch, to seize,’ not occurring in the NT) to learn something about someone, with the purpose of seizing, arresting, or overcoming
glosses: to learn in order to seize

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐγκόπτω ‘to knock in’ or ‘to incise,’ not occurring in the NT) to use strong measures in causing someone not to do something
to cause an offense to someone

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to a period of a hundred years
to cause to happen, with the implication of fulfilling some purpose
an important OT prophet
(derivative of ἐνδείκνυμαι[a] ‘to show, to demonstrate,’ 28.51) the means by which one knows that something is a fact
to enclose an object by winding something about or around it
to cause something to be in the shape of a roll
to be like or similar to something else
to possess more or less definite information about, possibly with a degree of thoroughness or competence
to come to an understanding as the result of ability to experience and learn
to acquire information, probably in a somewhat more exact or detailed form and perhaps with focus upon what is learned (compare 27.2)
senses.comment: ἐπιγινώσκω[c] also occurs in legal contexts referring to careful investigation and interrogation, as in Acts 22:24 and Acts 23:28.

senses.def: to identify newly acquired information with what had been previously learned or known
to indicate that one does know
senses.comment: It may also be possible to translate the expression in 1 Corinthians 16:18 as ‘you should give these people due recognition’ in the sense of ‘causing to be recognized’ or ‘causing to be acknowledged.’

senses.def: to care for or look after, with the implication of continuous responsibility
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐπισκοπέω in Hebrews 12:15, see 30.46.

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to give careful consideration to something, with the implication of guarding against
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐπισκοπέω in Hebrews 12:15, see 35.39. Some scholars have seen in the occurrence of ἐπισκοπέω in Hebrews 12:15 a meaning at least somewhat similar to that which occurs in ἐπισκοπέω[c] ‘to be responsible, to care for’ (53.70).

senses.def: to have responsibility for the care of someone, implying a somewhat official responsibility within a congregation
senses.comment: It is possible, however, that ἐπισκοπέω in 1 Peter 5:2 is not to be understood as designating some official responsibility but merely as a role of helping and serving (see 35.39).

senses.def: to suffer destruction, with the implication of being deserted and abandoned
pertaining to being straight in contrast to what is crooked

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being just and right

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: a straight road) the right or correct pattern of behavior

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time immediately subsequent to a previous point of time (the actual interval of time differs appreciably, depending upon the nature of the events and the manner in which the sequence is interpreted by the writer)
senses.comment: In Mark 1:21 εὐθύς probably implies what was done on the immediately following Sabbath. Accordingly, one may translate this expression in Mark 1:21 as ‘and on the next Sabbath he went into the synagogue and taught.’

senses.def: a seaport in the western part of the Roman province of Asia
the large celestial body that gives warmth and light to earth in the daytime
senses.comment: Translators have relatively few difficulties in obtaining a satisfactory term for the sun, though there may be a tendency in some languages to add some kind of honorific title to the word, for example, ‘our father the sun.’ Translators’ problems occur, however, with verbs describing the action or effect of the sun. For example, in Matthew 13:6, instead of speaking of ‘the sun rising,’ it may be more satisfactory to speak of ‘the sun shining’ or, in this particular context, possibly ‘when the sun was overhead’ or ‘by the time the sun had reached the sky.’ In Mark 13:24 one can perhaps best render the meaning as ‘the sun will no longer shine’ or ‘… will cease shining.’

senses.def: the one supreme supernatural being as creator and sustainer of the universe
senses.comment: The componential features of θεός involve a basic, underlying ambivalence. On the one hand, θεός is regarded as unique to the exclusion of all other gods: οὐδεὶς θεὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ‘there is no God but one’ 1 Corinthians 8:4. This is strictly a monotheistic view of θεός. On the other hand, there occur such expressions as εἴπερ εἰσὶν λεγόμενοι θεοί ‘even if there are so-called gods’ (1 Corinthians 8:5), and in the OT the Lord is described as being ‘far above all gods’ (), ‘the God of gods’ (), and the ‘great King above all gods’ (), which is essentially a henotheistic view of θεός. Fundamentally, however, the NT view may be most succinctly reflected in Galatians 4:8, τοῖς φύσει μὴ οὖσιν θεοῖς ‘those who by nature are not really gods.’ In other words, the gods of the pagans (see 12.22) are not to be viewed in the same category as θεός[a].|A further semantic problem is involved in the use of θεός[a] in reference to Christ. In John 1:1, the ‘the Word was God,’ the meaning of θεός may be described on the basis that all the componential features of θεός[a] are applied to the referent λόγος, which is in turn identified with ‘Christ.’ This is not to be interpreted as indicating that the two referents are identical (which was, of course, the position of those who maintained the so-called patropassian heresy), but that the distinctive features of θεός[a] are also fully applicable to another referent, namely, the λόγος or Christ; that is to say, it is legitimate to interpret John 1:1 as ‘the Word was God’ but not as ‘God was the Word.’|Translational equivalents of ‘God’ are of three major types: (1) proper names, (2) descriptive titles, and (3) borrowed terms. There are a number of problems involved in each of these types of translational equivalents.|If translators wish to employ in the biblical text a proper name in the receptor language, it is essential that the characteristics of the referent of such a name be sufficiently close to those which characterize the biblical God, so that the message may not be unduly distorted. In fact, the equivalent should be sufficiently close that ready identification can be made. The essential features of such a receptor language term should include (1) benevolent disposition and behavior, (2) creative and sustaining activity in the world, and (3) supreme power. In most instances it has not been found necessary for such a term to refer to a strictly monotheistic view (that is to say, having an existence which precludes the existence of any other gods), but it is essential that the name apply to a referent who is regarded as supreme over all others.|There may, however, be a number of difficulties involved in the use of an indigenous expression for θεός[a], since the views concerning such a god may involve such factors as (1) psychological distance (the idea that such a god, though all powerful, is still very remote from mankind) and (2) the necessity for constant propitiation (as though such a god needs to be constantly entreated or sustained by means of gifts in order to make him favorably disposed toward mankind).|In some instances problems have arisen in the use of an indigenous term for God because such a name may be perfectly appropriate in one area in which a language is spoken, but have quite a different meaning or value in another part of the language area. For example, in one area of East Africa the name for ‘God’ in one tribe is the name for the devil in a nearby, closely related tribe.|Descriptive titles for God (which often become essentially names) may focus upon a number of different features or characteristics. In some instances such descriptive titles are traditional for certain receptor languages. In other instances they have been constructed by translators on the basis of indigenous models. The following are illustrative examples of various types of descriptive titles: ‘he who made us,’ ‘the supreme powerful one,’ ‘the one who performs miracles,’ ‘the owner of all,’ ‘he who is sufficient,’ ‘our great father,’ ‘the highest one,’ ‘the great spirit,’ ‘the unending spirit,’ ‘the commanding spirit,’ ‘the great chief,’ ‘the self-existing one,’ and ‘the truly sacred one.’|Some Bible translators have attempted to avoid semantic complications by borrowing a term from a dominant language. In Latin America, for example, many early missionaries borrowed the Spanish term Dios, but in explaining the meaning of Dios as the great and all-powerful creator, they simply provided another name for what people already understood to be the sun. The difficulty with borrowed proper names is that they are essentially zero in meaning, that is to say, they are words with a significant absence of meaning which must be filled in one way or another, and this is usually done merely by equating the meaning of such a zero term with already existing concepts. Hence, rather than avoiding wrong views of God, borrowed terms often perpetuate wrong views indirectly.|There may also be additional complications in the use of a borrowed term, since it may not provide a basis for certain syntactic or morphological modifications. For example, some missionaries have borrowed the term Allah for ‘God,’ but in speaking of ‘gods’ they have attempted to add a plural to the underlying form Allah. In most instances this procedure has resulted in something which is not only conceptually and grammatically impossible, but also highly offensive to receptors.|One special problem involving θεός[a] results from the occurrence of ‘God’ in expressions of possession, for example, ‘my God’ or ‘our God.’ In a number of languages one simply cannot say ‘my God,’ for one cannot ‘possess God.’ Rather, one must say ‘the God whom I worship’ or ‘the God in whom I trust.’ Similarly, it may be impossible to speak of ‘the God of Abraham’ without implying that such a God would only be an idol, that is to say, ‘the God that Abraham personally possessed.’ Under such circumstances it may be necessary to translate ‘the God of Abraham’ as ‘the God in whom Abraham trusted.’|Ideally, one should employ a well known receptor-language term for ‘God’ which would be applicable not only to the one supreme being, but could also refer to the ‘gods of the heathen,’ that is to say, a rendering of θεός[a] should be a generic expression which could be made particular and even exclusive by some such qualifier as ‘the’ or ‘the one’ or ‘the unique.’ Sometimes this can only be done by a qualifier such as ‘the great’ or even ‘the supreme.’

senses.def: any one of many different supernatural beings regarded as having authority or control over some aspect of the universe or human activity
senses.comment: Some translators have made a practice of trying to render the meaning of θεός[b] by terms which mean essentially demons or evil spirits, but this is a mistake, for though the gods of the ancient pagans may be regarded as having had no existence at all, nevertheless, the NT does not speak of them as being evil.|In those languages in which there is no contrast between ‘gods’ and ‘spirits,’ that is to say, in instances in which people believe only in indwelling spirits rather than in supernatural beings who have control over natural phenomena, it may be possible to distinguish ‘gods’ by speaking of them as ‘powerful spirits.’ In certain instances, therefore, the equivalent of ‘God’ (12.1) is ‘the all-powerful Spirit.’

senses.def: a female deity
senses.comment: In some languages it may seem quite strange to attribute female sex to a divine being. However, one can almost always say ‘a woman god’ or ‘a spirit like a woman’ or ‘a spirit thought of as being like a woman.’

senses.def: (a title applied to Jesus, literally: son of God, parallel in semantic structure to phrases consisting of υἱός followed by the genitive of class or kind; compare 9.4) one who has the essential characteristics and nature of God
senses.comment: Before adopting a translation of υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ such as ‘Son of God,’ one must always investigate the extent to which such an expression might already be used in a particular language. For example, in the Tarahumara language of Mexico mankind is divided into two classes: (1) ‘sons of God,’ who are Tarahumaras and (2) ‘sons of the devil,’ all other people. In these circumstances it is necessary in translating υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ to use an expression which will identify ‘the unique Son of God’ or ‘the one who is truly the Son of God.’

senses.def: that which is offered as a sacrifice

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the poisonous secretion of some animals
glosses: poison (used especially of the venom of snakes)

senses.def: the substance resulting from the slow oxidation of metals (rust in the case of iron and tarnish in the case of gold and silver)
senses.comment: Pure gold is not affected significantly by oxidation, but much of the gold of the ancient world was not pure, and therefore oxidation and resulting tarnish did take place. However, in most languages it is inappropriate to speak of ‘rust’ as occurring with gold and silver. If there is no satisfactory term to indicate the deterioration in gold and silver resulting in extreme tarnish, it may be possible to translate James 5:3 as ‘your gold and silver will be ruined and this will serve as a witness against you.’

senses.def: to cause something or someone to be lowered or brought down
senses.comment: For another interpretation of καθαιρέω in Mark 15:36, see 15.199.

senses.def: to bring something down from one point to another
senses.comment: For another interpretation of καθαιρέω in Mark 15:36, see 15.110.

senses.def: to destroy completely by tearing down and dismantling
senses.comment: It may be important in rendering Luke 12:18 to indicate clearly that there is purpose in tearing down the barns, and that presumably materials resulting from the dismantling of the barns would be used in building bigger ones.

senses.def: to destroy by conquering and overpowering
to cause a state to cease
to cause something to be covered over and hence not visible

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: to cause something not to be known
to throw someone or something down a cliff

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: to use a seal to close or to make something secure
senses.comment: For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved with ‘seal,’ see 6.54.|From the immediate context of Revelation 5:1 it is not possible to determine whether the scroll in question had seven seals on the outside or whether the scroll was sealed at seven different points. However, since according to chapter six of Revelation the seals were broken one after another, it would appear as though the scroll had been sealed at seven different places as it had been rolled up.

senses.def: talk which lacks significant content
senses.comment: ‘Foolish talk’ may often be expressed as ‘to talk the way fools talk’ or ‘to talk with a smirk on the face.’

senses.def: a specially marked pebble, piece of pottery, or stick employed in making decisions based upon chance
senses.comment: Both in form as well as in function, the closest equivalent of κλῆρος[a] is frequently a term which refers to dice. In Luke 23:34 a term for dice would be particularly appropriate.|It is not possible to know the particular method employed in ‘choosing by lot,’ for evidently various devices were used. In Acts 1:26 (ἔδωκαν κλήρους αὐτοῖς ‘they drew lots,’ literally ‘they gave them lots’), it is probable that small sticks were handed out. See also footnote under κληρόω.

senses.def: that which is given as a rightful possession (often in the sense of an inheritance)

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: a responsibility, function, or ministry which has been assigned to a person
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κλῆρος in Acts 1:17, see 63.18.

senses.def: what has been assigned as someone’s responsibility to take care of
a share or portion which has been assigned or granted
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κλῆρος in Acts 1:17, see 37.101.

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the lot falls upon someone) the process of choosing, with the probable implication of discerning God’s will in this manner
senses.comment: In some societies the closest natural equivalents of deciding by lot are procedures involving ‘drawing straws’ or ‘throwing dice’ or ‘throwing down sticks’ or ‘dropping pebbles.’

senses.def: (derivative of Κόρινθος ‘Corinth,’ 93.506) a person who lives in or is a native of Corinth
to move around an object
senses.comment: A strictly literal translation of the Greek text of Hebrews 11:30 may be extremely difficult, since it is usually necessary to employ an active form involving movement so as to specify what entities go around. Therefore, it may be preferable to translate ‘the walls of Jericho fell after the Israelites had gone around them for seven days.’

senses.def: to move in such a way as to encircle an object
to not possess something which is necessary
to be lacking in the sense of not being in someone’s possession
senses.comment: For another interpretation of λείπω in Luke 18:22, see 71.33.

senses.def: to be a continuing obligation
senses.comment: For another interpretation of λείπω in Luke 18:22, see 57.44.

senses.def: a province in the interior of Asia Minor
a son of Ἰωσήφ[a] and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a marker of linkage in discourse
marker of relatively weak emphasis
glosses: indeed or frequently not translated but possibly reflected in the word order

senses.def: a marker of two or more items which are additively related and thematically parallel
a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another
glosses: on the one hand … but on the other hand

senses.def: a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another
glosses: on the one hand … but on the other hand

senses.def: a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another
glosses: on the one hand … but on the other hand

senses.def: combination of the negative particle μή[a] ‘not,’ 69.3, and the postpositive conjunction δέ[a] ‘and,’ 89.94
combination of the negative particle μή[a] ‘not,’ 69.3, and the postpositional particle δέ ‘even,’ which does not occur with this sense as an independent graphic unit in the NT
the only entity in a class
the only item of a class in a place
a particle marking a constituent as representing a limited number of entities
a particle marking a proposition as a condition, and so limiting the scope or impact of what was stated before by making it dependent on another event
a particle marking a proposition as contrastive, and so limiting the scope or impact of what was stated before
to signal to someone by means of part of the body, especially by means of the head or hands
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to types of gestures or motions of the head or hands and arms. For example, in John 13:24 there is an obvious question involved, and this may require in some languages a particular signal by means of the hands or face. The same would be true in the case of Luke 1:62. In Luke 1:22 the gesture would have to be something which would explain or indicate Zechariah’s inability to speak, while in Luke 5:7 quite another gesture would no doubt be called for, since the persons involved were at quite a distance from one another.

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: the period between sunset and sunrise
darkness of the night in contrast with daylight (see 14.40)
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret νύξ in Revelation 22:5 as a period of time rather than as darkness (see 67.192). See also ἡμέρα 14.40 and its footnote.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα - literally, forty days and forty nights) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
senses.comment: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (expressions, literally: night and day, day and night, respectively) duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits
to regard something as presumably true, but without particular certainty
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to suppose’ or ‘to presume’ is ‘to think somewhat’ or ‘to think perhaps’ or ‘to think a little.’ In some instances the lack of certainty is spelled out clearly as ‘to think, but not with certainty’ or ‘to think, but not to know’ or ‘to think, but not to be sure.’

senses.subdomain: In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
senses.def: a position behind an object or other position
marker of one who is followed as a leader (occurring with a variety of verbs indicating change of state or movement)

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a marker of a point of time closely associated with a prior point of time
a marker of strongly emphatic negation
the totality of a relatively large group
to rebel, with the implication of provoking to anger
glosses: to rebel and provoke to anger

senses.def: (derivative of παρρησία ‘boldness,’ 25.158) to speak openly about something and with complete confidence
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to speak boldly’ is ‘to speak regardless of who is listening’ or ‘to speak without fearing’ or ‘to speak without worrying.’

senses.def: to have courage or boldness in the face of danger or opposition
to look or to glance around, though not necessarily in a complete circle
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to look around’ would be ‘to look in one direction and then in another’ or ‘to keep on looking in different directions.’

senses.def: moistened earth of a clay consistency
senses.comment: πηλός contrasts with βόρβορος ‘watery mud’ (2.17) and refers to moist earth with a consistency of clay. It may be translated in some languages as ‘sticky soil’ or ‘clay-like mud’ or ‘moist dirt.’|In Romans 9:21 (ἢ οὐκ ἔχει ἐξουσίαν ὁ κεραμεὺς τοῦ πηλοῦ ‘or doesn’t the man who makes the pots have the right to use the clay as he wishes’) the reference is specifically to potter’s clay. The meaning of πηλός, therefore, may be defined as any kind of moist earth with clay consistency. πηλός includes the area of meaning of κέραμος ‘potter’s clay’ (a meaning not occurring in the NT).|Since pottery is so widely known throughout the world, there is normally no difficulty in obtaining a term which refers to potter’s clay. Even when the making of pottery is not known, it is usually possible to obtain a satisfactory term for such clay, for example, ‘mud that can be molded’ or ‘mud for shaping pots.’

senses.def: pertaining to that which exists in a large amount, with the implication of its being valuable
a high point on any scale and having the implication of value as well as abundance
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to preserve the figurative meaning of ἐκχέω in Titus 3:6; therefore, one must render this expression as ‘whom God caused us to have in an extensive manner’ or ‘whom God caused us to have very much of.’

senses.def: the color purple; has the symbolic value of royal status)
senses.comment: In John 19:2 the use of πορφυροῦς may refer more to the symbolic value of the color than to the color itself. Therefore, it may be important to include some marginal note indicating the significance of the color.

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a reddish-purple cloth dyed with a substance obtained from the murex shellfish; expensive to produce; associated with wealth and royalty
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no special color term for reddish-purple, since the color in question is sometimes classified as a kind of blue and in other instances it is related to black. However, in all languages it is possible to be somewhat more precise about color terms by likening the color to that of a local flower or bird.

senses.def: to announce with certainty in advance as to what one will do
to cause something to be fixed in place by means of nails
one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause something to move back and forth rapidly, often violently
senses.comment: In some languages there are quite distinct terms for shaking, depending upon the vigor of the motion and/or the objects which are shaken. Accordingly, one must exercise care in selecting terms which will accurately and adequately represent the nature of the shaking in the various contexts. For example, in Hebrews 12:26 the shaking would presumably involve some kind of reverberation, but in Revelation 6:13 the action of the wind suggests whipping something back and forth.|It is possible to interpret σαλεύω in Matthew 24:29 (αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν σαλευθήσονται ‘the hosts of heaven will be shaken’) as meaning literal shaking, but it may be used figuratively in the sense of deposing the hosts of heaven from their positions of power.

senses.def: to cause people to riot against
(a figurative extension of meaning of σαλεύω ‘to shake,’ 16.7) to become emotionally unsettled and distraught

smallish brown or gray moth that lays eggs in clothing or other cloth; eggs hatch into very small caterpillars, which feed on the fibers; Tineidae family, probably Tineola biselliella; symbols of decay, ruin, and slow destruction
senses.comment: In the NT the Greek term σής is used only in reference to the larvae of moths, and therefore it is frequently necessary to employ a term in the receptor language for the larvae rather than for the flying insect. This means that frequently an appropriate equivalent is ‘the worms of moths,’ but often one can employ an expression which means simply ‘cloth worms’ or ‘cloth eaters.’|In Matthew 6:19 the effect of the larvae of moths is combined with rust as agents for the destruction of valuable objects. It is rare, however, that one can speak of the destruction caused by moths in the same way as one can describe the effects of rust or tarnish. It may therefore be necessary to talk about ‘moths eating cloth,’ while ‘tarnish ruins precious metal.’

senses.def: worthless or unwanted material that is rejected and normally thrown out
to keep oneself away from some activity
purposely to avoid association with someone
glosses: to have nothing to do with

senses.def: to be counted as belonging to a particular group

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a group of persons engaged in eating together
senses.comment: Note that Luke employs κλισίας in essentially the same type of context in which Mark uses συμπόσια.

senses.def: a pattern of behavior more or less fixed by tradition and generally sanctioned by the society
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no noun for ‘custom’ or ‘habit,’ but the same meaning is communicated by verbal aspects or adverbial phrases indicating habitual action. For example, in the case of John 19:40 one may translate in some languages ‘as is the way in which Jews always bury people,’ and for 1 Corinthians 11:16 one may translate ‘this is not what we constantly do.’

senses.def: to split or to tear an object into at least two parts
senses.comment: In some languages the meaning of σχίζω in Mark 1:10 may be best expressed as ‘the sky tore’ or ‘there was a slit in the sky’ or possibly ‘there was suddenly an opening in the sky.’ The adverb ‘suddenly’ may provide some of the implications of the splitting involved in the verb σχίζω.

senses.def: to split or divide into two parts

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being perfect in the sense of not lacking any moral quality
senses.comment: Compare the meaning of τέλειος[e] mature in 88.100.

senses.def: pertaining to being truly and completely genuine
pertaining to having no defect whatsoever
pertaining to that which is fully accomplished or finished

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being mature in one’s behavior
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret τέλειος in Ephesians 4:13 as meaning ‘perfect’ (see 88.36).|In Matthew 5:48 it is possible that τέλειος also means maturity of behavior, but it is usually interpreted as ‘being perfect,’ since the comparison is made with God (see 88.36).

senses.def: pertaining to an adult human being
senses.comment: Though in Hebrews 5:14 τέλειος is to be understood in a literal sense, the context as a whole is figurative.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: one who is initiated into a religious community of faith (a meaning which reflects the occurrence of τέλειος as a technical term for persons initiated into the mystery religions)
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘initiated’ (Philippians 3:15) may be best expressed as ‘to become a member of’ or ‘to become a believer in.’ It is possible, however, to interpret τέλειος in Philippians 3:15 and Colossians 1:28 as mature spirituality or a state of being spiritually mature (see 88.100).

senses.def: the interest on money that has been loaned
to be more abundant than a given quantity
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὑπερπερισσεύω in Romans 5:20, see 78.34.

senses.def: an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in 78.31 primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
senses.comment: Though it is possible to interpret ὑπερπερισσεύω in Romans 5:20 as referring simply to quantity (see 59.49), it is better to interpret it as expressing degree. χάρις itself indicates the activity of God in showing favor, and ὑπερπερισσεύω is simply an expression of abundant degree involved in such an activity.

senses.def: a location above the earth and associated with supernatural events or beings
senses.comment: The parallelism in the phrases peace in heaven and glory in the world above indicates quite clearly the equivalence in reference, though not in meaning, between οὐρανός[b] (1.11) and ὕψιστος[a].|In Matthew 21:9 the phrase ὡσαννὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίστοις, literally ‘hosanna in the highest,’ has been interpreted as a plea for salvation or deliverance from God who is in heaven. However, it seems preferable to understand ὡσαννά as simply being a shout of exclamation or praise and therefore to interpret the phrase ὡσαννὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίστοις as meaning ‘praise to God.’ In Luke 19:38 a parallel expression, καὶ δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις, literally ‘and glory in the highest,’ is usually understood as an acclamation of glory to God and therefore may be so rendered. See 33.357.|In contexts in which these expressions refer clearly to ‘heaven’ or ‘the sky,’ it is better to use terms meaning ‘heaven’ or ‘sky’ rather than terms meaning ‘height’ or ‘that which is high.’

senses.def: (a title for God, literally: highest) one who is supreme, primarily a reference to status
senses.comment: In some languages the concept of height is entirely unrelated to the idea of importance, and therefore it may be necessary to translate ‘the Most High’ as ‘the Most Important’ or even ‘the Greatest.’

senses.def: a city in Macedonia
senses.comment: For Καισάρεια τῆς Φιλίππου 'Caesarea Philippi,' see 93.492

senses.def: to hold someone or something in close custody
to continue to obey orders or commandments
to make a distinct effort to keep oneself from doing something
glosses: to make an effort not to

senses.def: to be on one’s guard against some eventuality
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a great deal of difference in terminology employed in speaking about guarding an area in order to apprehend someone and guarding a flock of animals for fear of theft from robbers or danger from wild animals.

senses.def: cardinal number, where there are one thousand instances of a countable entity
one who utters falsehoods and lies
senses.comment: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’
